tldr: By automatically extracting occupancy costmaps through voxelization and semantic goal candidates via multi-view segmentation from fixed 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) scenes, the authors built "NavArena," a high-quality benchmark for closed-loop navigation evaluation.
hero_caption: Overall pipeline of NavArena. It integrates egocentric visual rendering (visual layer), occupancy costmaps (spatial constraint layer), and object instance candidates (semantic layer) from fixed 3DGS models to enable reachable, collision-free episode generation and unified closed-loop evaluation.
overview:
Faithfully capturing the real world, 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) enables fast and photorealistic novel-view synthesis, leading to the rapid accumulation of large-scale scene datasets. However, because 3DGS is merely a collection of visual appearance primitives, it lacks traversability boundaries, collision queries, reachable goals, and a unified closed-loop evaluation environment. Consequently, it could not be directly used as a navigation benchmark. Previously, manual mesh repairing or per-scene semantic optimization was required, which posed a major bottleneck for large-scale scaling.

To address this, the authors developed "NavArena," an automated framework that derives the spatial and semantic interfaces required for navigation from fixed 3DGS assets. NavArena delegates visual rendering to a frozen 3DGS model, estimates an occupancy costmap as the spatial layer based on Gaussian opacity and robot height constraints, and lifts and fuses 2D open-vocabulary masks into 3D to establish a semantic layer of object goals. This creates an environment that uniformly supports PointNav, ImageNav, and ObjectNav without requiring conversion into full physics simulators or per-scene retraining.

Applied across more than 2,000 diverse scenes, NavArena successfully generated 22.2 million reachable and feasible expert trajectories. Furthermore, compared to a mesh baseline (FCL) across 100 scenes, it achieved roughly 8x to 11x faster collision checks while maintaining zero false negatives, alongside a semantic goal accuracy of 92.25%. Zero-shot closed-loop evaluations using existing navigation policies demonstrated that the unified protocol clearly uncovers issues often overlooked by distance-only success metrics, such as heading misalignment and failures in issuing explicit STOP actions.
contributions: Proposed an automated method to derive traversability, collision queries, and semantic goal candidates directly from fixed 3DGS models without manual mesh repairs or per-scene semantic optimization.

Established a unified closed-loop evaluation pipeline for three navigation tasks—PointNav, ImageNav, and ObjectNav—under shared action spaces, observation formats, termination criteria, and evaluation metrics.
Automatically generated 22.2 million expert trajectories across more than 2,000 diverse scenes, demonstrating high scalability and reproducibility as a large-scale evaluation foundation.

sections.heading: Visual Realism Isn't Enough: The Missing Link to Turn 3DGS into Navigation Environments
sections.summary: While 3DGS renders photorealistic environments at high frame rates, it lacks collision checks, traversable areas, and valid goals. NavArena proposes an approach to automatically extract the spatial and semantic layers needed for closed-loop evaluation from fixed 3DGS scenes without building full physics simulators.
sections.details:
In goal-oriented visual navigation, closed-loop evaluation is essential: an agent must act based on its observations, receive new viewpoints as it moves, avoid obstacles, and reach designated coordinates or objects. Conducting this properly requires not just realistic visuals, but also traversable boundaries, collision feedback, reachable goals, and consistent termination and success criteria.

Recently, 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) has made high-quality novel view synthesis possible at practical rendering speeds, leading to the collection of large scene repositories. However, these are pure appearance models lacking explicit free space, collision boundaries, and verified goal coordinates. Existing pipelines attempt to reconstruct meshes, construct NavMeshes, or optimize per-scene semantic fields, but no general method existed that could be applied automatically to uncurated, large-scale 3DGS assets.

The authors asked: "Can fixed 3DGS models be automatically augmented into reproducible closed-loop evaluation benchmarks without turning them into full physics simulators?" NavArena keeps the frozen 3DGS strictly for observation rendering (visual layer), while extracting an occupancy costmap from Gaussian geometric statistics (spatial layer) and lifting goal candidates from open-vocabulary segmentation back-projections (semantic layer). This enables the unified evaluation of PointNav, ImageNav, and ObjectNav under a single interface without manual mesh repairing or additional training.

sections.heading: How Does It Differ from Prior Simulators and 3DGS Research?
sections.summary: Existing navigation benchmarks rely on curated meshes or specialized simulator annotations, and prior 3DGS works focused on rendering integration or per-scene training. NavArena specializes in automatically generating evaluation benchmarks from fixed, uncurated 3DGS assets.
sections.details:
### II-A Goal-Oriented Navigation Benchmarks and Simulators
Traditional navigation evaluation platforms (such as Habitat, Gibson, AI2-THOR, and ThreeDWorld) assume meticulously curated meshes, simulator-specific annotations, or procedurally generated assets. While these allow strictly controlled evaluation, applying them to generic reconstruction models not built specifically for simulation is difficult. NavArena fundamentally differs by directly deriving navigation interfaces from fixed 3DGS models that were not pre-conditioned for simulation.

### II-B 3DGS-Based Embodied Environments
An increasing number of studies apply 3DGS to robotics and Embodied AI. For instance, Gaussian rendering has been embedded into existing simulators, and coupled with physics engines or robot learning backends. However, their primary focus is rendering integration or individual physical dynamic simulation, rather than providing a framework to automatically transform arbitrary fixed 3DGS assets into benchmarks for goal-oriented navigation.

### II-C Semantic Grounding for Object Navigation
For ObjectNav, some methods distill vision-language features into Gaussians or optimize semantic fields on a per-scene basis. However, these are computationally expensive and ill-suited for large-scale scaling. NavArena adopts a paradigm of lifting and fusing multi-view segmentation masks into 3D, eliminating per-scene training entirely. Furthermore, instead of dense semantic scene understanding, it applies specialized filtering tailored for benchmark construction: reliably retaining reachable and collision-free goal candidates.

sections.heading: A Unified Scene Representation Decoupling Visual, Spatial, and Semantic Layers
sections.summary: Instead of turning scenes into complete physical environments, NavArena decouples them into 3DGS for visual rendering, an occupancy costmap for collision and traversability queries, and object goal candidates. This allows robust evaluation without requiring watertight meshes or rigid-body physics.
sections.details:
In NavArena, each transformed scene is treated not as a complete physics simulator, but as an evaluation asset $\mathcal{S} = (\mathcal{G}, \mathcal{M}_{\mathrm{occ}}, \mathcal{I})$. Here, the roles of each component are completely decoupled:

- $\mathcal{G}$ (Visual Layer): The frozen 3DGS model dedicated to rendering egocentric RGB and depth observations.
- $\mathcal{M}_{\mathrm{occ}}$ (Spatial Layer): The occupancy costmap used for reachability and collision queries.
- $\mathcal{I}$ (Semantic Layer): A set of labeled 3D object instance center coordinates providing goal candidates for ObjectNav.

By decoupling these roles, NavArena avoids the need for closed polygonal meshes (watertight meshes) and complex rigid-body physics engines, sidestepping geometric artifacts common in raw reconstructions.

A benchmark instance is defined as $\mathcal{B} = (\mathcal{S}, \mathcal{D}, \Pi)$, where $\mathcal{D}$ includes episodes, trajectories, and goals, and $\Pi$ specifies action spaces, termination conditions, evaluation metrics, and the closed-loop protocol. Integrating them into a shared geometric coordinate frame allows diverse scenes and tasks to be evaluated under a single, standardized protocol.

sections.heading: Automatically Building Navigation Spaces from Gaussian Opacity and 2D Masks
sections.summary: By voxelizing Gaussians and aligning them to the ground plane, NavArena estimates a 2D occupancy grid tailored to the robot's height. Furthermore, by back-projecting multi-view SAM3 masks, voxel voting, and clustering, it precisely identifies object goal centers without additional training.
sections.details:
### IV-A Overview
Taking a frozen 3DGS $\mathcal{G}$, camera poses, and a list of object categories as input, NavArena performs coordinate normalization, height-aware occupancy inference, valid region estimation, and semantic grounding. Given an agent pose $q_t$, the rendering function yields an RGB-D observation $(I_t, D_t)$, while the transition function determines whether movement via control input $u_t$ is collision-free via $\mathcal{M}_{\mathrm{occ}}$.

### IV-B Spatial Constraint Inference
The spatial constraint layer is constructed through the following steps:
- **3DGS Voxelization**: The contribution $\rho_{i,\nu}$ of each Gaussian to a voxel $\nu$ is calculated from its opacity and Mahalanobis distance. These are fused as independent occupancy evidence into an effective opacity $A_{\nu}$, which is binarized with a threshold $\tau_{\mathrm{occ}}$. Color and spherical harmonics are ignored, extracting geometric shape only.
- **Coordinate Normalization**: Using RANSAC on occupied voxels, the dominant supporting plane (floor) is detected. Its normal is aligned with gravity, and the floor is placed at $z=0$ via a rigid body transformation, aligning scenes from heterogeneous sources to the same coordinate frame.
- **Occupancy Map Inference**: Voxels intersecting the robot body's height interval $\mathcal{H}_{\mathrm{body}} = [h_{\min}, h_{\max}]$ are flattened into a 2D grid of occupied cells, producing a map tailored to the robot's physical dimensions.
- **Valid Region Estimation**: After filtering floating noise via DBSCAN, an $\alpha$-shape concave hull is computed from horizontally projected points to determine the support mask $M_{\mathrm{sup}}$ where reconstruction data exists. Combining this with obstacle inflation by the robot radius $r_{\mathrm{agent}}$ yields the final navigation costmap $\mathcal{M}_{\mathrm{occ}}$. Regions lacking data are excluded as unknown space.

### IV-C Semantic Grounding for ObjectNav
The semantic layer is constructed without training (Training-free):
- **Frame-Level Semantic Extraction**: RGB-D views rendered from the Gaussians and category names are fed into SAM3 to obtain 2D semantic masks. To suppress boundary noise from semi-transparent Gaussians, the masks are eroded, and pixels with valid depth are back-projected into 3D point clouds using camera geometry.
- **Scene-Level Semantic Fusion**: Per-frame point clouds are voxel-downsampled and merged, followed by majority voting across a coarse grid. Voxels lacking sufficient multi-view support or having conflicting labels are discarded. The confirmed labels are transferred to Gaussian centers, and DBSCAN clustering is performed to obtain center coordinates $\mathbf{x}^{\mathrm{obj}}$ for each object instance. Because benchmark construction prioritizes avoiding false positives (invalid goals), this design strictly optimizes for precision.

captions.F2: Figure F2: Training-free semantic grounding process for ObjectNav. Starting from per-view SAM3 mask erosion and back-projection, it performs multi-view aggregation via voxel voting, transfers labels to Gaussians, and identifies object centers via clustering.

sections.heading: Unified Task Generation and Closed-Loop Evaluation
sections.summary: NavArena automatically generates reachable, safety-verified episodes and expert trajectories for PointNav, ImageNav, and ObjectNav. During online evaluation, standardized action, collision, and termination models ensure fair comparisons across policies.
sections.details:
### V-A Task Definition
An episode is defined by an initial state $q_0 \in \mathrm{SE}(2)$, a task-specific goal $\gamma_{\mathrm{task}}$, and an expert trajectory $\tau^{\star}$. The three tasks differ only in their goal format and success criteria:
- **PointNav**: A metric 2D target coordinate $\mathbf{x}_{\mathrm{goal}}$.
- **ImageNav**: A reference image rendered at a reachable target pose.
- **ObjectNav**: An object instance belonging to a specified category extracted in the semantic layer.

### V-B Episode Generation
An initial pose $q_0$ is sampled from the valid region, and a goal is assigned. Candidate pairs are accepted only if they satisfy distance, reachability, and collision constraints. An expert trajectory $\tau^{\star}$ satisfying kinematic constraints (clearance and continuous turning) is then synthesized on $\mathcal{M}_{\mathrm{occ}}$. Because observation images are rendered dynamically online, episodes are stored compactly as metadata and trajectory files.

### V-C Closed-loop Evaluation Protocol
During evaluation, agent action $a_t$ is converted into relative waypoints $(\Delta x, \Delta y, \Delta \theta)$, collisions are verified against $\mathcal{M}_{\mathrm{occ}}$, and the pose is updated. Two termination protocols are supported:
- **Distance-based**: Automatically marks success and terminates the moment the agent enters the goal success radius.
- **Explicit-stop**: A stricter protocol where entering the radius is insufficient; the agent must explicitly emit a $\mathrm{STOP}$ action inside the radius to succeed, while calling $\mathrm{STOP}$ outside results in failure.
Goal distance thresholds are uniformly evaluated as planar Euclidean distances in the shared coordinate frame.

### V-D Evaluation Metrics
Standard evaluation metrics include Distance-based Success Rate (Distance SR), Explicit-stop Success Rate (Stop SR), Success weighted by Path Length (SPL), Navigation Error (NE), Collision Rate (CR), and Average Steps (AvgSteps). For ImageNav, Pose SR is also evaluated to assess orientation alignment at the goal.

sections.heading: Evaluated Across 2,000 Scenes and 22.2M Trajectories: Speed, Accuracy, and Policy Diagnostics
sections.summary: Spatial queries were roughly 8x to 11x faster than FCL with zero false negatives, while semantic center accuracy reached 92.25%. Closed-loop policy rollouts revealed significant performance drops over longer horizons and severe weaknesses in explicit stopping and heading alignment.
sections.details:
### VI-A Experimental Setup
The benchmark encompasses over 2,000 scenes from InteriorGS (~1,000 scenes), SceneSplat++ (~1,000 scenes), and custom real-world captures (50 scenes). Evaluated models include PointNav (LoGoPlanner), ImageNav (GNM, ViNT, NoMaD, NaviBridger), ObjectNav (PoliFormer, Uni-NaVid, OmniNav), and generalist multi-task models (NavDP, OmniVLA), tested across 600 shared episodes per track split evenly into Easy (180), Medium (240), and Hard (180).

### VI-B Spatial and Semantic Validity
Across 100 scenes containing ground-truth meshes, NavArena's grid queries were compared to the standard collision library FCL:
- **Spatial Layer**: The occupancy grid at $0.05\,\mathrm{m}$ resolution was 7.91x faster for state checks and 10.72x faster for motion checks compared to FCL. The false-negative (FN) collision rate during motion checks was 0%, guaranteeing safety. The $0.05\,\mathrm{m}$ resolution retained accuracy comparable to $0.025\,\mathrm{m}$ while reducing memory usage from 382.4 KiB to 61.6 KiB.
- **Semantic Layer**: Compared against manual annotations across 10 scenes, NavArena achieved a valid object center rate of 92.25%, significantly outperforming baselines (SceneSplat at 65.95% and FlashSplat at 57.36%). This highlights how mask erosion and strict voxel voting prevent false positives.

### VI-C Dataset Scale
NavArena automatically generated 22.2 million expert trajectories (over 160,000 hours of navigation time) across more than 2,000 diverse scenes, producing a 3DGS navigation dataset of unprecedented scale for both training and evaluation.

### VI-D Closed-loop Diagnostic Utility
Closed-loop rollouts revealed distinct behavioral characteristics across policies:
- **Overall Performance**: In single-task ImageNav, NaviBridger achieved top performance (Distance SR: 0.508, CR: 0.040), while Uni-NaVid led ObjectNav (Distance SR: 0.567, SPL: 0.354).
- **Horizon Degradation**: As tasks grew longer from Easy to Hard, success rates degraded across all models. ImageNav models suffered steep drops of 72% to 91%, illustrating how perceptual and local control errors accumulate over long horizons.
- **Sensitivity to Termination Protocols (Key Insight)**: Episodes deemed successful under distance criteria dropped by roughly 49.1% to 62.5% when evaluated with orientation alignment (Pose SR) in ImageNav. More strikingly, in ObjectNav, requiring an explicit stop action (Stop SR) caused success rates across all evaluated policies to collapse below 0.05. This demonstrates high diagnostic utility: modern policies can easily get near a target, but struggle immensely to recognize the goal and bring themselves to an intentional stop.

sections.heading: Conclusions and Outlook: From Static Scenes to Dynamic Worlds
sections.summary: NavArena establishes a scalable framework for automatically building navigation benchmarks from fixed 3DGS assets. Currently limited primarily to static environments and planar SE(2) motion, it remains dependent on the underlying reconstruction quality.
sections.details:
NavArena successfully automates the end-to-end construction of goal-oriented navigation benchmarks from large-scale 3DGS assets by decoupling and coordinating three layers: visual (3DGS), spatial (occupancy costmap), and semantic (lifted instances). This allows multifaceted diagnosis in closed-loop settings, including success rates, collision rates, degradation across long horizons, and the success of explicit stopping behaviors.

However, the authors acknowledge several limitations:
- **Mobility Model**: The framework currently focuses on static indoor environments and planar $\mathrm{SE}(2)$ motion, without supporting vertical step climbing or uneven 3D terrain.
- **Dependence on Input Quality**: Visual rendering and geometric fidelity depend heavily on the quality of the input 3DGS. Incomplete reconstructions risk missing occupancy cells or producing false-positive obstacles.
- **Policy-Specific Adaptations**: Mapping model outputs to standardized waypoints may cause slight deviations from each model's native performance on physical hardware.
Future work points toward expanding into environments with dynamic obstacles and supporting robots with higher degrees of mobility.

takeaways: Decoupling visual appearance (3DGS) from physical and geometric constraints (occupancy grids) allows building fast and accurate navigation environments without watertight meshes or full physics simulators.
Evaluating beyond distance-based success—specifically checking orientation alignment (Pose SR) and autonomous stopping (Stop SR)—uncovers major bottlenecks in modern navigation models.
Combining 2D open-vocabulary mask erosion with voxel voting enables precise 3D object goal localization (over 92% accuracy) without any per-scene training.
limitations: The robot mobility model is restricted to planar movement (SE(2)), which does not support steps, stairs, or uneven 3D terrain.
Performance depends on the quality of the input 3DGS reconstruction; severe capture artifacts or unobserved areas can degrade the derived spatial and semantic layers.
Mapping policy outputs to standardized waypoints for evaluation may slightly deviate from the models' native performance on real physical platforms.
